newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's lower house approves 1997 tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Germany's lower house approves 1997 tax bill.

text.p: Germany's lower house on Thursday passed a compromise version of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 tax bill approved by a parliamentary mediation committee earlier in the day.
Approval of the measure had been delayed for weeks by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who hold a blocking veto on tax measures through their control of the upper house.

But the SPD finally caved in on scrapping the wealth tax rather than bow to a government threat to allow the bill to fail. Tax increases worth over eight billion marks were agreed last week to cover losses from the wealth tax.

Deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition voted for the compromise, the SPD abstained and the smaller opposition parties -- the Greens and reform-communist Party of Democratic Socialism -- voted against.

Waigel, keen to get German finances into shape for Europe's planned economic and monetary union, welcomed the compromise agreed by the mediation committee. "The government has implemented its main tax policy goals," he said.
The upper house is due to vote the bill into law at its last pre-Christmas session on Friday of next week.

Despite the bill's approval, the coalition remains at loggerheads with the opposition over government plans to abolish company capital trading taxes in western Germany. These taxes are not included in the tax bill.

Hermann Otto Solms, the parliamentary leader of the junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, offered to hold talks with the SPD over the Christmas parliamentary break to find a compromise on the issue.
